comments.name: Henry Lieberman
comments.body:
Prof. Bruni,

You don't have to feel guilty for "draining students' transcripts of
meaning". They are already devoid of meaning. And it wasn't your
fault. As a university teacher, your job, like mine, is to help
students learn and develop as thinkers and scholars. You are under no
obligation to act as a screener for companies with lazy HR departments
or hiring managers who want a quick filter, and who can't be bothered
to learn who their applicants really are.

The best way to help students learn is to work with them to
develop their intrinsic love of learning and the subjects you are
teaching. They have to believe you are on their side. The worst thing
about "tough grading" is that it makes students believe that education
is a work-for-grades transaction, and that they are in an adversarial
relationships with you. If they get into a transactional
mindset, then of course they seek to do the least work for the highest
grade.

You have to convince them that *you* care more about getting them
interested and helping them with achievements in the field than in
making them sweat, or judging them. Tough grading undermines that.
You don't have to give As to a flunking student, but be generous with
grades. Treat grades (as the students do) as an externally-imposed
annoyance that you both have to deal with, without letting it consume you. 
Make the classroom interaction be about the learning that
both you and your students are doing, together.

It is up to the professor to create a course that is appropriately challenging so that students have to “stretch” and, and in doing so, some students will rise to meet those expectations and others may not—and grades should reflect that across a spectrum that the professor has explained clearly in the syllabus:  A= excellent, B=very good, C=good/satisfactory, etc.

comments.name: Ignacio Götz
comments.body: Beautifully put, Ms. Gay, and accurate, as far I can tell. I have a suggestion for the more traditionalist democrats who fear the dismantling of the "old party" they have been used to: USE the old structures, the old institutions, but DON'T BELIEVE IN THEM. Used them like you'd use a pair of shoes you discard when they wear out. Don't get fixated on the structures, but only on the goals. Because, in truth, it's the goals that count; the structures are just tools to obtain the goals, and as everybody know, you fit the tools to the objective, to the goals: you don't build a house with a tractor, or use an iron beam to cross the Atlantic. This idea comes from Ortega y Gasset, the Spanish philosopher. He called it "institutional atheism," the disbelief in institutions that would render it easier to get rid of them, or modified them as the need arises, in order to obtain the goals. The goal is the good of the people, whether it is called left, right, center, socialist, progressive -- whatever: it's our welfare that is at stake, our health, our spirit, our aspirations, our companionship, our generosity toward each other, our kindness, especially toward aliens from other lands and climates, mindful that we are all HUMAN.

I very much hate to say this, but I hope the US Navy is up to the task. The Navy’s most powerful vessel, the aircraft carrier Gerald R. Ford, is now undergoing repairs in Norfolk, Virginia. The ship was deployed for 326 days, but repairs following a major onboard fire are expected to take over a year.  The ship will be out of service, at a time when it is badly needed in the Middle East,  likely for a longer period than its deployment.

Over the past two decades, the Navy has lost two modern warships to fire, the atomic submarine Miami, and the amphibious assault ship Bonhomme Richard. Both fires were started by single rogue individuals while the ships were docked at bases in the continental US.  Both ships had to be decommissioned because the fires could not be quickly extinguished.

As the Navy plans for the future, building more large warships may not be the best approach.  Instead, building many smart, nimble vessels designed for today’s drone-based warfare may be the better option. Establishing bases on land at more friendly countries around the world is likely to be essential, especially given the issues with the Ford.

The Navy needs to be prepared to fight tomorrow’s wars, not yesterday’s.  And the Navy badly needs to develop and deploy technology that can manage fires onboard ships, lest our warships become sitting ducks during battle.

So someone going into public safety service at 22 years of age can retire (at or near full salary) in their early to mid fifties.  They may draw benefits for a longer period than they worked.  You don't see the same conversations about health insurance benefits because they often aren't even funded.  Just paid in full every year for life.

I see some commentors stating that this can be changed.  For some inexplicable reason in some states the courts have gotten behind this and said that public employee pensions can't be touched.  Without exaggeration there are decisions saying that if a 22 year old fireman is hired today, they are guaranteed that their pensions can't be altered (downward).  Ever.

These abominations happened in the late 1980's and early 1990's when the unions lied to elected officials (and bribed them with contributions) saying that "hey look at our graphs" the stock market will always go up and all of this pays for itself.   Yup.  That's what happened.

Bit of a tangent, but here is the effect of Trump's war of choice on existing shipping costs (i.e. pre 'guardian' toll):

MARINE INSURANCE:  Before the war the average premium was 0.25% of the replacement value of the hull. Now ordinary cargo ships are paying 1% of hull value. Premiums for tankers or US-flagged vessels range now from  face 7.5% to a whopping 10% of hull replacement value (from Loyds London)  That means a new supertanker could wind up paying up to $30 mn for war risk insurance for the region. For a single voyage.

CHARTER RATES:  If you need to charter a tanker to ship your cargo of crude from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, you will pay between $400,000 to $800,000 DAILY depending on the size of the vessel. I can't remember ever seeing charter costs this high.

In sum, even before Mr Trump's proposed 'guardianship fee', his misbegotten war has already imposed significantly higher costs for the delivery of crude oil.

comments.name: dsws
comments.body:
The quoted poll question conflates open "primaries" with better options such as ranked-choice voting.  

A primary is an election by which a party chooses its nominee.  Open "primaries" are a type of preliminary, not primary,  election.  More importantly, they create bad incentives.  

Suppose there are two parties: the yellow party, preferred by 60% of voters, and the purple party, preferred by 40%.  Suppose further that the purples believe in open participation, while the yellow party values organization and careful vetting. Four purple candidates step up, while the yellows recruit two.  In each party, the votes are split almost evenly.  So each yellow gets about 15% of the vote, and each purple gets about 20%.  The general election features two purples and no yellow, to the frustration of a majority of voters, because the purple party responded correctly to the incentives it faced, while the yellow party didn't.  

A preliminary system forces parties to be control freaks, even if (like the yellows in my example) they would prefer not to be.

comments.name: E
comments.body: There are two separate issues: (1)the process by which a given party chooses who gets to run on its ballot line in the general election=a primary in most cases, but not necessary - some use caucuses or conventions (2)the structure and rules of a general election. (1)is a private matter of political parties. (2)is a matter for the state and the electorate and they should be kept separate. The state could just institute 2-round voting, like they have in multiple countries. The parties could still run whatever process they want to choose a candidate (or two) eligible to run in that general election. If the general electorate has significantly different views from party loyalists, it may be better to produce 2 candidates rather than one for the general, with some discrepancy in their positions. The general election usually proceeds from first to second round by the top 2 or 3 vote getters proceeding to the final round. A ranked choice avoids the multiple rounds by allowing people to express their 2nd, 3rd, etc choice. A lot of the comments here appear to be from dedicated party followers who assume that independents are low information voters. I would ask them to rethink this position as most of the independents I know vote in every election and all were members of some party or other in the past. They are better thought of as disillusioned with both parties, unable to map their heterodox beliefs neatly into either party platform, and more interested in choosing individuals.

Were any people touching the produce after it was washed washing their hands frequently and/or changing gloves?   What about the food prep in the restaurant.   These are food-chain inspection questions.  The current administration is bent on destroying an already-inadequate system. 
I don't buy salad mixes, and I'm a bit leery of salads in restaurants.  At home I refresh greens under running cold water and soaking them for 15 minutes or so, separating what I need for that meal, inspecting and rinsing under the tap, then allowing the them to drain dry in a colander.
Then I drain the head, wrap in a clean towel and store in a plastic bag.  I use the same procedure on garden produce.

Given the potential harms, AI companies must face litigants in court. Judgments could force the AI company into bankruptcy. Or they should be nationalized by the government. No matter how much money they have or they spend, it will not buy them an authentic experience or the passion shared by the true fans of this game. Every time this has happened in my experience, I acknowledge it for what it is to that person, they acknowledge that, yes, its special, and then I thank them for it happening in my presence. Then it's over. Then soon after, they depart. This is why I say it's been a privilege to care for someone who is dying. Although it's very hard and exhausting,  I would not trade that experience.

comments.name: Alice Know
comments.body:
I’ve known paradoxical lucidity and  terminal lucidity. Art therapy produced paradoxical lucidity for one Alzheimer’s patient; later, nurses learned she’d been an art teacher. 

Covid protocols produced a moment of terminal lucidity for another Alzheimer’s patient who’d been silent for years; her husband had joined her in nursing home living by then, and he’d raised his voice to near-shouting to chat through their open 3rd story window with his daughter on the grounds below. This patient then also called out to her daughter and had an entire conversation, “A miracle” her daughter told me. The patient died a few days later. 

Both incidents seemed strongly stimulus-response in nature to me, but the context included a combination of factors that might not have been reproduced easily. In particular I took the terminal case to be a result of gathering energy to struggle against a final and irreversible decline. I’ve had two kids and it seemed like childbirth energy to me, that burst of energy in a pregnant person that makes older folks say whoa, I think that kid will be out here with us in the next 24 hours. 

My first thought reading this article was, wow, now maybe terminal lucidity will be included in the list of warning signs shared with loved ones to spend more time and make their goodbyes.

comments.name: NS
comments.body: I have been a caregiver for two people who died of dementia: my stepmother and my husband. Both of them often had episodes of lucidity. It was confusing and upsetting for me as I tried to cope with their decline. Dementia is a personality changer, and not for the better. I have come to believe that the incidents of lucidity were simply random inexplicable events. My stepmother stopped speaking months before she died, but even in her final coma, she seemed to wait for my sister and her daughter to arrive before she died, and then to die after we had left her room. My husband remained verbal until his death. His last words to me, as he rolled up the covers as if he were going on a ride, were: "Now the worries are yours."

comments.name: Deanna Jacobs
comments.body: My grandfather Howard was a brilliant man, a literature scholar, a polymath, a beloved teacher, and the finest raconteur I ever met.  After a number of TIA's, he slipped into a mental fog and mumbling silence, sometimes tapping at his temples and winching at his failure to make connections and retrieve memories.  He and  I were very close and I wasn't ready to lose him.  Then one morning, when we were "talking" on the phone--I would pretty much do all the talking--he was suddenly his old self again and could remember everything, inquiring after my wife, my young daughter,...  With my wife looking on at me across the kitchen table, I emotionally told him how he had been for the last couple of years and he had no real recollection of it, his response being "That is remarkable."  My wife, who was a veterinarian, cautioned me that this lucidity sometimes happens before people die, and sure enough, he did die soon afterwards. (PMJ)

comments.name: Gareth Wong
comments.body:
This letter is right that the clock is the real risk but the more urgent question isn't whether AI takes your job, it's whether anyone can catch what an AI system is about to do before it acts.

In December, an Amazon AI coding agent decided the quickest fix to a bug was to delete and rebuild a live production system: 13 hours of outage. Amazon called it a permissions oversight, not a rogue AI but that's the problem.

These systems already make consequential, irreversible decisions faster than the humans supervising them can react. That's not about job displacement; it's about whether AI can be reliably overseen in real time.

NIST scientist Apostol Vassilev published a peer-reviewed proof this year showing no fixed set of safety rules can fully guarantee that (arxiv.org/abs/2512.10100) a mathematical ceiling, not a patchable gap. 

A UC Berkeley benchmark this year found frontier agents pass barely 2.6% of real, economically valuable tasks (arxiv.org/abs/2606.05405)  the capability gap this letter assumes closed isn't close to closed.

And today's AI pricing is subsidised, NOT real cost. 

Uber ran that playbook: price below cost until the taxi trade broke, & by the time the true cost was visible, the industry was gone +much of that workforce landed in precarious gig work instead. 

We're sadly debating the labour seating chart on a plane whose autopilot isn't proven safe yet and whose ticket doesn't reflect what the flight costs to run.

comments.name: Heather

The paradox of A.I. is that it encourages humans to use their brains less—which makes them lose their literacy and critical reasoning—but A.I. needs literate users who can provide critical feedback because it’s not fully human.

It’s as if we built powerful machines freeing us from backbreaking work, but the only way to turn on those powerful machines is by being as fit as an Olympic athlete!

Imagine if a bulldozer could only be turned on via a crankshaft that required the driver to exert a force comparable to bench pressing 200 pounds!

If this paradox happened with machines, everyone would need to go to the gym to build the strength required to turn on their car or their laptop!

So, will humans need to go to “brain gyms” in order to be savvy enough to interact well with A.I.?

Or will A.I. continue to improve to the point that human oversight and feedback will be unnecessary?

In my experience creating A.I. prompts, my conclusion is that—in the near term, at least--humans will need to up their mental game! Those who don’t will allow A.I. to do many foolish things.

comments.name: Hopsong
comments.body:
OK, let me get this straight:
--A new housing project is going on blighted land, and that's bad because...
--Global warming. But New York is best place for more people to live for environmental reasons (transit, etc). But it's still bad because...
--It's in a flood plain. Another developmental project got flood protection so it's not fair...
--But this project is going to have a flood wall, too. But that's bad because...
--An archetect says we should live closer to the water...
--Which already floods and killed a person...
--In another neighborhood.
People really, really (cross my heart) want more housing...
Just not here...and not this big...and maybe not this many poor people...and...and...

This article is one-sided: it does not adequately engage with the benefits of new housing development in one of NYC's highest-demand neighborhoods. Instead, the article should have dug into the actual facts of the Monitor Point development, rather than platforming NIMBY perspectives dressed up as empirical fact. I expect more from The New York Times.

comments.name: Z
comments.body: Six hundred foot towers? What insanity is motivating this fiasco? Obviously money and greed. With global warming it is imperative to avoid high rises which contribute to the "heat island" effect. If you must build more housing, limit the height to four stories high and don't build in an area where flooding is likely to occur. Turn that land into a park with trees instead of building towers. More trees equal less carbon dioxide in the air.

comments.name: DD in LA
comments.body:
“ Using private funds, Gotham will pay for and execute tasks that the authority, the city and other groups had agreed to perform more than 20 years ago…”

There it is, the crux. 
Maybe if the city had kept its promise, the area would have been today a nicely designed recreation area. But through laggard stewardship, it falls on private entities to clear the area and, surprise, they’re doing it for their own development profits

comments.name: Const
comments.body:
It seems that no piece of open space is spared once developers see an opportunity to build. Every park, waterfront, field, or vacant parcel becomes another potential construction site. It is discouraging to watch green space steadily disappear, especially in dense urban areas where it is needed most.

When I read about declining populations in the U.S. and many other countries, I see one potential long-term benefit: less pressure to pave over the remaining natural areas. Perhaps, over time, we can slow—or even begin to reverse—the loss of open space and better preserve the environment for future generations.

comments.name: Ouch
comments.body: Let's be clear, because this article isn't: Residential development and park development are NOT mutually exclusive. Quite the opposite, just look at Brooklyn Bridge Park. These living spaces for our fellow humans will NOT be built on park land, but next to it. They will, however, make the waterfront accessible, as in other parts of Williamsburg and Brooklyn. The answer to a changing environment can't be to say not to new development, but to use resilient tactics to ensure that, when flooding happens, the water has places to go without destroying buildings and infrastructure. Stop the NIMBYs!

comments.name: Trob
comments.body:
Two thoughts:
1. NYC does a terrible job of putting up massively tall buildings on the waterfront. They should stack them as they go back to allow for air flow but also neighborhood development. Buildings further back will be talled and still have some view of the water which is more valuable and thus better at generating tax revenue and 'spreading the wealth. Currently one large building goes up and all the ones behind instantly lose value

2. I am curious who will be paying insurance for these developments.  There are many in NYC that have lost their homes both to storms and the cost of insurance against them.

comments.name: Doug Hassebroek
comments.body:
I live within the nameless twenty-block stretch of Flood Zone 2 surrounding Bushwick Inlet, where Williamsburg and Greenpoint meet. The area was badly flooded during Hurricane Sandy in 2012. In acreage, it is roughly comparable to Manhattan’s Two Bridges neighborhood, which was also severely inundated and will soon benefit from the floodwalls of the East Side Coastal Resiliency project. In population, however, we are surely not equivalent to Two Bridges -- yet.

I do not expect a comparable floodwall project to be built around Bushwick Inlet anytime soon. But in my estimation, the likelihood increases, however slightly, each time a project such as Monitor Point is erected.

"If we need to raise significant capital to pursue an expansion, we need to determine the expansion will more than pay for itself.  Two primary options are open to us.  We can take on debt (either a bank or issue corporate bonds) or sell treasury stock.  If we decide to either borrow from a bank or issue corporate bonds, it is because the Board of directors have determined that the interest we are going to pay is substantially less than the market value the stock should appreciate after the expansion.

He had elbow inflammation, which, in the end, didn't require TJ surgery. But the orthopedic doctor who examined him asked some tough, borderline inappropriate questions about whether he was really that injured (MRIs showed some issues, yes, but they were open to interpretation). He eventually explained that some kids - high schoolers! - were willing to undergo TJ surgery, because even back then, recovery was such that you'd come back with increased velocity, at least in the immediate aftermath of recovery. Blew my mind then, and now, where, as we know, it's common for elite pitchers to undergo TJ procedures twice during their careers. Mind boggling. (It was a rotator cuff injury, now the last automatic career-ender, that closed out his playing career).

In short, the scientific method involves entertaining all possible explanations while attempting to disprove as many as possible. It's iterative and can eventually prove things by exhausting all alternatives and it involves being able to keep an open mind while holding multiple possibilities aloft.

Meanwhile, the most likely explanation for the rise of skeletal muscular injuries in athletes this decade is shut out from the discussion. Perhaps people's cell biology and biochemistry knowledge is too inadequate to even know it's a player, but I suspect we're intent on actively ignoring this particular thing that does widespread harm well beyond mere sports injuries.

To fast-track recruits, basic training was slashed from 72 days to 42, cutting out 240 hours of instruction. They quietly eliminated tests on gun safety and use-of-force. Worse, Schwank testified that instructors were actually ordered to teach recruits they could enter private homes without a warrant—a direct violation of the Fourth Amendment.

This created deep anxiety inside the academy. Both veterans and young recruits panicked because they felt totally unprepared, yet they were graduated anyway just to get bodies on the street. Ultimately, Schwank quit out of a profound dread of the real-world results, warning that sending thousands of undertrained officers onto the streets would inevitably lead to unlawful arrests and tragic mistakes.

comments.body: From ‘61-‘67, my grandfather, a Seventh-Day Adventist preacher working for the Southern Publishing Assn, spent most of his time on extensive preaching tours. At that time the Adventist churches were segregated. When he was in town, on Sabbath he would usually preach at BOTH the white and the black churches—black churches last, as they had much longer services. He has never attacked, but it was dangerous. He carried an unloaded and unusable sawed-off shotgun in his car. Once he had to put it out his window, resting on the mirror, when a group of white men with clubs and bats blocked the road to stop him. They moved. He went on to the next city.

comments.name: Steve M.
comments.body: Ed King showed  a lot of courage in a dangerous time. Don't forget that most of the white people of Mississippi who violently opposed civil rights for black people in the 1960s went on to support the Republican Party and its candidates in Mississippi. And, those who are still living are avid MAGA fans.

comments.name: vsr
comments.body: I grew up just north of what was then still called the Mason-Dixon Line. Black friends and neighbors venturing south of the line into Maryland for work had to eat meals in restaurant kitchens or in the cabins and beds of cargo trucks, the dining rooms denied them by segregationist laws and practices. A white boy, I was astonished. Maryland has changed to a solidly Blue State since then, but to think that segregation existed in my lifetime -- all those years after the Emancipation Proclamation and the Civil War -- saddens me. Now, with a President openly fanning the flames of racism, I am all the more persuaded that racism per se is evil and must be beaten back constantly, like pulling weeds in a summer garden. As a boy, I admired the Ed Kings. They were the brave gardeners of decency and civility, and gave me hope of a better world. They still do.

Of all the threatened elements of our environment, dark skies require special vigilance.

As a global concern, preserving them is not only about beauty; the diurnal rhythm of the sky affects living things, including us, and we can't be fully healthy without night.

The trouble is, each individual instance places that concern far down on the priority list. THIS military post, THIS shopping center, THIS oilfield... each represents a different pattern of planning, review and approval, and each time, advocacy for dark sky preservation takes a back seat if it gets any notice at all. Or it's derided as a niche concern among "bigger things."

The sky is the biggest thing. We're killing the night sky one lamppost at a time, when there are easy mitigations available for those who care to listen.

Funny watching the comments here fume as if backroom access and connected getting first crack at public money is some unique Trump invention. It isn't, though he does it with a certain panache. It scales with the size of government itself, and federal outlays have grown from about $4.1 trillion in 2018 to over $7 trillion now, 70% growth, so the ecosystem around that money has grown right along with it.

This article proves the point,  a CEO admitting he had to build "a government lobbying company" just to compete for a Navy contract, investors with inauguration donations and White House ties landing meetings ordinary bidders never get. That's just the current administration's version.

The last administration had its own. The EPA's Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund handed $20 billion of a $27 billion pot to eight nonprofits in the final months, several newly formed with no track record, staffed by former Obama and Biden officials. One EPA appointee was caught on tape comparing the rush to get the money out before the transition to "throwing gold bars off the Titanic." Reviewers flagged financing plans like $358,000 per electric vehicle.

Solyndra, PPP fraud, cost-plus defense contracting that rewards overruns instead of punishing them. Different party, different press release, same mechanism: concentrated benefits for whoever is connected, massive costs for whoever is paying taxes.

Why do this?  Mainly to save on energy costs and get rid of the ancient oil tank in my basement.  But the bigger reason is for my kids.  When they get this house they'll be able to heat and cool it affordably, and the air-conditioning will be able to keep up when it's 120f and 90% humidity.

Many people don't realize that this mass extinction is already well underway. It's happening across animal populations, plant life, and our oceans. Too much attention is focused solely on rising air temperatures, as in this article. But Earth is a water planet, and we should be paying at least as much attention to the temperature and health of our oceans. They regulate our climate, support most life on Earth, and are showing alarming signs of stress.

So what did our government do? It cut funding for ocean monitoring equipment and the agencies responsible for tracking and reporting these changes—precisely when we need that information the most.

Entry lines were stretched longer than usual. It wasn’t until I got inside that I realized the concert wasn’t starting until around 10 PM. In a situation like that you stay locked in. Safety is non-negotiable.

Thank God nobody got hurt and nothing went sideways that could’ve ended with arrests. Jay-Z took the stage and personally apologized to the fans inside Yankee Stadium. That kind of direct accountability? Real respect for that.
The show finally lit up at 12:15 AM and rolled strong until about 3 AM.

What really stood out: New York City Transit kept those event special trains running well after the final note — pushing deep into the hours when most services are normally secured. That’s operational professionalism. That’s how you move a city and get people home safe.  It is particularly enjoyable to ride in a new R211 subway train.

I’ll take safety every time. No exceptions.

I am a doctor practicing in Kolkata for the last 12 years. About 30% of the patients presenting at a clinic near the airport had Bangladeshi roots. They were both Hindus and Muslims. The migration is entirely economic for the Muslims but for the Hindus, the reasons were mixed. Many Hindus reported religious persecution but I took those claims with a pinch of salt. The migration had happened through the 1970's, 80s and so on up to the recent years. Many of them displayed their Bangladeshi as well as their official Indian residency documents. These documents are generally issued to citizens of the respective countries, even though their value in legally evidencing citizenship claims have been recently challenged in India. Many had families on both sides of the border and they would frequently cross the border with the most suitable documents available. Some of these people initially came to India with valid visas and overstayed for decades. Many slipped in undocumented with the help of people smugglers. 

This is a personal experience and not a systematic well designed population level study but we were 10 doctors in the clinic with identical experience and the senior ones were not at all surprised.

If my experience could be generalized, we are talking millions, likely tens of millions. So, a political backlash was expected and perhaps, long overdue.

I fully support closed borders and stopping all illegal immigration which also helps to stop illegal contraband. There can be room for legal application for asylum but that has gotten out of hand in too many places.

A LIFE SENTENCE

Meet Frank Sayer, a fabled fabulist who stops to shop at an ordinary bookstore. Frank ponders the meaning of ‘vagary’ in a red, rhyming dictionary. What Frank doesn’t know is he is about to wander into a world he never expected: the rhyming zone of The Twilight Zone.

Frank finds himself in reverie. A place so wonderfully savory: the smells of a bakery, a cakery, a yummy muffin makery — but the baguettes and bagels are papery pages of fakery. 

In an act of bravery unwavery, Frank pulls back the velvety drapery. Suddenly, the dream turns unsavory. Topsy-turvy. Unnervery. Frank is in the rain, in pain, in chains — a prisoner in an era of America’s slavery. Frank is trapped forever in his mind’s rhyming chicanery.

I hope Singapore's leaders recognize that freedom of expression isn't just about fostering world-class journalism. It's also what allows great art, theatre, films, television, and literature to flourish.

Hong Kong became the center of Chinese-language popular culture in the 1970s–1990s because it enjoyed a high degree of freedom of expression under British rule. Likewise, South Korea's global cultural influence accelerated after democratization and the liberalizing reforms of the late 1990s, creating an environment in which creative talent could thrive.

If Singapore aspires to become a true cultural hub, this is worth reflecting on. Censorship in the name of defamation charges can stifle creativity of all kinds.

My varicose veins disappeared and have stayed that way in the 30+ years since.   I have since cut back to 500 mg. per day. 

AI Overview:
"Vitamin C is essential for vein health because it supports the production of collagen and elastin, the connective proteins that keep vein walls firm, elastic, and capable of proper blood flow..."

"Collagen Production: It is a vital building block for creating and maintaining the structural integrity of vein walls and valves."

"Antioxidant Properties: As a powerful antioxidant, it helps reduce the inflammation and oxidative damage associated with chronic vein issues."

In my experience, vitamin C can indeed eliminate varicose veins, plus it works wonders on aging skin, for the same reason: collagen production.

comments.name: Dee
comments.body:
Varicose veins are the result of an underlying issue- chronic venous insufficiency- and not an independent issue. The procedures to treat them involve injecting superglue into bad/closed vein, or radiofrequency or laser ablation (they are eventually  absorbed by the body). These are the top two ways now; stripping - removing the vein- is not a preferred method of treatment currently.
None of this addresses the issues of bad valves in one's veins, so more varicose veins are likely in future. How to lessen future issues?  The genetics of whether one is prone to this and/or hormonal changes are out of one's hands, but the things people can control: wear compression stockings always, elevate legs often; lose weight; no smoking. Move often- sitting for long spells is the worst. Exercise regularly, especially to build calf muscles to help pump blood back up the leg.

The law is still the law. The Fair Housing Act has been approved by Congress, signed by a president, and upheld by federal courts for nearly 60 years. But it has been weakly enforced under all presidents, with minor ups and downs, before enforcement nearly completely stopped in this administraiton. Yet, it's still the law. State fair housing laws also still are in effect. Most enforcement has fallen to fair housing groups such as the ones that did the testing described in this article, though the federal government through HUD has tried to cut their funding as well.

comments.name: Ana Ionova

I decided to travel to Parintins to show a different side of Brazilian popular culture, going beyond the Carnival celebrations the country is known for. I had heard that the bull, and the rivalry over it, was central to Amazonian identity, and I wanted to see it up close to understand what it meant to people there.

What I found was that this tradition had a lot to do with people’s desire to preserve their complex history, which mixes Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian folklore with traditions brought over by colonial settlers. While reporting in Parintins, I was also struck by how, despite people’s impassioned allegiances, the rivalry was mostly civil and respectful. This stood out to me, given how polarized Brazil is right now in other realms like politics and ideology.

articles.title: Red Bull or Blue Bull? In This Brazilian Town, You Have to Choose.
articles.summary: Deep in the Amazon rainforest, a heated rivalry has split a town for a century. It’s got nothing to do with sports or politics.

They kept growing food as if they still had seven children living with them, and kept three root cellars fully stocked. (Does anyone build root cellars in basements anymore? Does anyone build basements?) Much of what I read here is old European knowledge. Start things indoors early. Compost all you can. Rotate. Plant garlic in the fall so it comes in during the spring, then plant a leaf crop there for early fall salads. Etc., etc. a side benefit - my grandmother was still bent over her plants at 92, still growing to feed a family of nine…we should all be so lucky….or is it common sense?
